profiles.title: Systems Approaches to Making Change
profiles.canonical_definition: A practical guide by Martin Reynolds, Sue Holwell and Patrick Hoverstadt presenting a range of systems approaches for making systemic improvement in complex situations of change and uncertainty.
profiles.summary: A practice guide presenting multiple systems approaches as resources for improving complex situations rather than as rival brands from which one must be chosen permanently.
profiles.why_it_matters: It connects Patrick Hoverstadt's work to Martin Reynolds and Sue Holwell and gives the atlas a public route from systems-method diversity to practical change.
profiles.key_distinctions: ["approach repertoire vs universal method", "systemic improvement vs implementation programme", "practice guide vs complete field history"]
profiles.historical_lineage: ["Open University systems practice", "critical systems thinking", "management cybernetics"]
profiles.common_misreadings: ["five approaches cover the whole field", "tools are interchangeable without assumptions"]
profiles.open_checks: ["review the full contents and map each approach precisely", "add case-level evidence"]
profiles.editorial_note: Developed from cited public sources. The entry remains open to correction, rival accounts and stronger evidence.

profiles.title: David Ing
profiles.canonical_definition: Systems researcher, educator and practitioner whose work connects service systems, systems thinking education, pattern language, systems changes and the documentation of systems lineages.
profiles.summary: Ing’s work is useful in two ways at once: he develops service-systems and systems-changes approaches, and he leaves unusually inspectable public trails through systems scholarship, teaching and institutions.
profiles.why_it_matters: The atlas needs lineages that are documented rather than merely asserted. Ing’s publication archives, teaching records and ISSS work connect contemporary practice to longer systems traditions while also contributing his own approaches.
profiles.key_distinctions: ["service systems are relational rather than reducible to service transactions", "systems changes are not assumed to follow unfreeze-change-refreeze", "documented association is weaker than demonstrated intellectual influence", "systems traditions are plural and historically situated"]
profiles.historical_lineage: ["ISSS leadership and systems-sciences community", "service systems science", "systems thinking education", "pattern-language research", "Systems Changes Learning Circle"]
profiles.logical_antecedents: ["systems sciences", "service science", "Gregory Bateson’s ecological epistemology", "Christopher Alexander’s pattern language", "learning and action inquiry"]
profiles.dependent_subsequents: ["service systems thinking teaching", "Systems Changes Learning", "pattern-language experiments for services", "lineage-rich public systems archives"]
profiles.practice_connections: ["teaching systems thinking", "learning circles", "service-system inquiry", "public documentation of conferences and sources"]
profiles.common_misreadings: ["Treating Ing only as a documenter misses substantive service-systems and systems-changes work.", "Treating a documented connection as proof of influence overstates what an archive can establish."]
profiles.open_checks: ["Add more independent scholarship evaluating the service-systems and systems-changes contributions."]
profiles.editorial_note: Public account based on named sources; documentary provenance, interpretation and evaluative claims are kept distinct.

profiles.title: Systems Thinkers
profiles.canonical_definition: A biographical history of thirty systems thinkers which relates lives, ideas, institutions and practice while providing a visible, challengeable selection of the field.
profiles.summary: A biographical history of thirty systems thinkers which relates lives, ideas, institutions and practice while providing a visible, challengeable selection of the field.
profiles.why_it_matters: The book is both an unusually useful map and an example of canon formation. Its authors explicitly examined the disciplinary and boundary choices involved in selecting key systems thinkers.
profiles.key_distinctions: ["biographical history versus timeless taxonomy", "thirty selected thinkers versus an exhaustive field", "life and practice versus ideas alone", "selection evidence versus later canonisation"]
profiles.historical_lineage: ["Open University systems teaching", "early cybernetics", "general systems theory", "systems practice and critical systems"]
profiles.common_misreadings: ["The book is not a final ranking of the field.", "The presence of a thinker is not evidence that every later practitioner was influenced by them."]
profiles.open_checks: ["Map all thirty chapters and their source extracts.", "Compare the 2009 and 2020 selections and revisions.", "Record serious omissions and rival canons as evidence, not as a corrected master list."]
profiles.editorial_note: The book's selection is represented as a documented and useful canon-making act, not as the natural boundary of systems thinking.

profiles.summary: Ramage connects systems history, sociotechnical information systems, critical inquiry and the active problem of who is allowed to count as a systems thinker.
profiles.canonical_definition: Ramage connects systems history, sociotechnical information systems, critical inquiry and the active problem of who is allowed to count as a systems thinker.
profiles.why_it_matters: His work makes canon construction part of systems practice rather than treating a list of recognised figures as neutral inheritance.
profiles.key_distinctions: ["biographical history versus a final canon", "documented selection versus natural category", "critical and decolonial inquiry versus adding decorative diversity", "sociotechnical systems versus technology-only explanation"]
profiles.historical_lineage: ["The Open University Systems Group", "systems thinking education", "sociotechnical information systems", "critical and decolonial curriculum work"]
profiles.dependent_subsequents: ["Systems Thinkers", "systems thinking from the margins", "decolonial systems education"]
profiles.common_misreadings: ["Treating Systems Thinkers as an objective ranking misses the authors' own boundary questions.", "Treating decolonisation as demographic decoration leaves the knowledge rules unchanged."]
profiles.open_checks: ["Add published outputs from the systems-thinking-from-the-margins work when available.", "Trace the Open University teaching lineage in more detail."]
profiles.context_and_lineage: Institutional and intellectual context: The Open University; systems history; sociotechnical information systems; critical and decolonial approaches. No ethnicity is inferred or assigned.
profiles.editorial_note: The profile records publicly stated intellectual and institutional context. Heritage and identity are included only where self-described, publicly sourced and relevant to the work.

profiles.summary: Shipp brought long experience of interactive and transformative systems education into the Systems Thinkers project and its people-centred account of the field.
profiles.canonical_definition: Shipp brought long experience of interactive and transformative systems education into the Systems Thinkers project and its people-centred account of the field.
profiles.why_it_matters: Her role prevents the book being treated as Ramage's individual classification exercise and connects canon construction to actual teaching practice at The Open University.
profiles.key_distinctions: ["co-authorship versus supporting role", "education and facilitation versus abstract history", "life-and-practice account versus disembodied ideas"]
profiles.historical_lineage: ["The Open University Systems Group", "interactive systems education", "facilitation", "Systems Thinkers project"]
profiles.common_misreadings: ["Reducing Shipp to a secondary co-author repeats the visibility problem the canon review is intended to expose."]
profiles.open_checks: ["Locate further public records of Shipp's systems teaching and facilitation work."]
profiles.context_and_lineage: Institutional and intellectual context: The Open University Systems Group; interactive and transformative learning; facilitation. No personal heritage is inferred.
